messages.subject: Complex ODE based Models
parts:
Dear Stan users,

We are currently working on facilitating Stan for ODE based models, see wiki. Developers working on the project seem to be mostly familiar with pharmacometrics and system biology. We would like to learn about other potential applications, and what users may be looking for. For more discussion on the subject, see this thread on the development list. 

Since this is posted on the user list, the discussion should really focus on users' needs. Implementation details should be discussed in the development list.  

Thank you for your help!

~ Charles

messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: Re: Complex ODE based Models
parts:
Thanks for the great news.

Few comments:

PBPK (physiologically based PK) models - which are extension of multi-compartmental PK models - are described both with ODE and algebraic equations or by DAE (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_algebraic_equation) in general. It might be worthwhile including this aspect.

Also, I have tried stan's ODE solver and it chokes when PBPK model is fed. There are techniques to solve ODE's in an approximate way - see orthogonal collocation "Numerical Solution of Differential Equations with Orthogonal Collocation" - but I saw some other techniques that are being used by stan users.

Linas

messages.subject: Re: Re[2]: [stan-users] Re: Complex ODE based Models
parts:
Hi Linas!

Have you tried the recent "bdf" integrator in Stan? That uses CVODES which is a very robust integrator specifically tailored for large ODE systems.

If you have a large ODE system and only want to estimate a few parameters, then make sure that all parameters which are held fixed are passed into the integrate function via the x_r argument. This is really important to keep things manageable.

Also: Do you have the Jacobians of your ODE RHS function available? If not consider using a package like dMod (on CRAN). Using dMod you will be able to generate automatically the Jacobian of the ODE RHS wrt to the parameters and the states. Once you have those, it is possible to supply these to Stan - if you are willing to put together a bit of C++. This is completely unsupported and an experimental use of Stan, but it can give massive speedups - I have done this approach myself and got about 3x speedup for a small 3 state system; for these large systems I expect even larger speedups. However, this all depends on getting the Jacobians right for which a tool like dMod is the only feasible way of doing it, I think. In case you want to try this approach I can share an example of a 2-cmt oral dosing situation where I use dMod to generate the code I needed.

Sebastian

parts:
The good part that not all parameters are of interest. The characteristics of organ, tissues and drug are described by physiological and compound-specific parameters. Physiological Parameters include arterial and venous blood flows, tissue volumes, tissue blood flow rates and tissue composition (lipid, phospholipids, and water).
Compound-specific Parameters include physicochemical properties (e.g. logP, pKa, dissolution rate) and biochemical/ biophysical properties (e.g. Vmax, Km, and permeability, fraction unbound in plasma or tissues, blood to plasma ratio). PK-derived Parameters are computed by combining compound-specific and physiological parameters, such as tissue-to-plasma partition coefficients (Kpu) estimated from logP, pKa and tissue composition and intrinsic clearance (CLint) derived from Vmax, Km and amount of liver microsomal protein. We are interested in PK parameters which may be estimated even from scarce data.

I will try to conquer my model using the outlined procedure. Hopefully I will be able to cite stan... Just for the heck of it the model is attached. Originally it was in C++ and was automatically translated directly to stan so there are lots of formatting issues.

Linas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Complex ODE based Models
parts:
I'm definitely interested in this effort.  I've used MCSim in the past, mostly for system dynamics models of the sort one might create with Vensim.  Perhaps the key special feature that requires is so-called tabular nonlinearities.  In MCSim, I'd use the GSL (not available here, I know) to interpolate between points.  You can see an example at https://www.gnu.org/software/mcsim/mcsimqrc.pdf.  Often, these models are simply used to generate simulation output, but they are also used to estimate parameters.  It would be nice to be able to do such modeling easily in Stan.  

Not long ago, I got called upon to do some hydrological modeling, and I came across conceptual hydrological models (PBPK for rivers?).  One important challenge is defining initial conditions--in this case, often moisture content in the layers of soil.  Those are, in general, unknown, but it's really handy to know boundary conditions when solving a system of ODEs. :-)  The way I think they get around this is through optimization--varying, for example, the initial soil moisture content until they get an output that matches real data.  Conceptually, that's easy to think of for a stream that runs dry in the summer: after some number of days with no precipitation and no flow, there is also probably no stored water, at least in the upper soil layers.  I'm obviously no expert here, but it would be nice to be able to handle such models, as well.

There are apparently other problems with conceptual hydrological models involving accuracy.  Some authors point out that it's low, partially because a river is a complex distributed system, and partially because they're often trying to calibrate a model with lots (for them--perhaps 50 or so) parameters with little real data--mostly precipitation, temperature, and river flow measured on a daily basis, but those are hard things to measure over a distributed area in the wild.

Bill

Bob,

That nonlinearity isn't used as a spline basis function.  In an ODE, the derivative is some function of the state of the system and any inputs, right?  The behavior of the system gets interesting, if that relationship between a state variable and a derivative is nonlinear.  A physicist might use a quadratic or some other analytic function to describe that relationship, while a system dynamicist would draw a function and then digitize key (x,y) points for the system to interpolate (I often have used Stineman interpolation).  You're at Columbia, right?  Check out a copy of Sterman's /Business Dynamics/; there's a whole chapter on nonlinearities.

Does that help?

As for the SIR model, you can find a chapter on the SIR model and its variants in Sterman, used there to model diseases, the diffusion of ideas, and the like.

Do you have any pointers to using Stan with unknown initial conditions?  That's what I was trying to get out in https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/ode$20initial$20conditions%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/mPIxQvGFZBM/46fRB2AmBQAJ, and I came away with the impression that it couldn't be done.

Bob,

Directly to your question about the model: there are no "inputs" to this model, at least in the MCSim sense.  sir.model defines the dynamics of the system: states, outputs (to expose them), and initial values of parameters and states. It then defines the dynamics, akin to the ODE function call, and it defines calculated outputs, akin to generate quantities in Stan.  The system starts in an initial state that's not in equilibrium, and it progresses towards equilibrium.

sir.test01.in should be obvious except perhaps for two aspects.  Each Simulation{} section defines a new run of the model, and each PrintStep defines when it will produce output (variable name plus the arguments to something like R's seq()).  (There's also a Print statement that lets you define specific times.)

Bill

Bob,

Look at the example on p. 2 of the two-pager I linked to.  Pretend "Balance" is what you have in a savings account, and "desiredOutflow" is what you intend to spend a month on, say food at restaurants.  You add nothing to that Balance ever.

The model as show continuously draws 100 per unit time from that balance, but that can't go on forever; the bank will shut it off at 0.  In order to approach 0 smoothly, as you might do in practice, we have an "EffectOfLowBalance" that is 1 when the balance is high (so it doesn't affect desiredOutflow), and it declines smoothly to a constant fraction of Balance when Balance gets low.  That is, at high Balance, outflow is constant; at low Balance, outflow is a constant times the remaining Balance.  The transition is smooth, thanks to the GSL interpolation.

Yes, that's a spline.  No, that's not a basis function AFAICT.  It's part of the likelihood, if you will, if I were only doing estimation, but I'm doing forward simulation.

Does that help?

Bill

unknown.  Anyway, Stan supports any combination of known and
unknown parameters and initial conditions.  We don't support
